title: The Expert Who Shapes the Law
hook: Lawmakers regulating a product they do not understand call a scientist. Whether that scientist's travel was paid for by the industry is not a detail — it is the whole reliability question.
key_points: Legislatures rely on outside experts precisely because they lack in-house technical knowledge, which gives a single credible scientist real policy leverage.
Disclosure rules exist because the audience cannot independently check whether funding shaped the testimony — they can only weigh it if they know about it.
Per ProPublica, University of Florida professor Christopher McCurdy testified in Arkansas, Rhode Island and Georgia, briefed Congress, and presented to a UN commission urging that kratom stay legal.
ProPublica reports he did not disclose travel reimbursements from the American Kratom Association, the industry's main lobbying group, including an $8,700 first-class ticket.
The university's policy requires disclosure above $5,000 in annual travel; ProPublica reports he listed none, and the university said it found no indication of non-compliance.
McCurdy said his positions come from more than two decades of research and are not dictated by the association, and that reimbursed expenses do not change his conclusions.
content_html: When a legislature regulates something technical — a drug, a chemical, an algorithm — it does not have the expertise in the room. It borrows it. That borrowing is normal and necessary, and it is also the point where interested money can enter a policy debate wearing a lab coat.
extra_html: ProPublica's Anjeanette Damon reports that Christopher McCurdy, a University of Florida pharmacy professor, became a leading scientific voice urging policymakers to keep the plant substance kratom legal, testifying before legislators in Arkansas, Rhode Island and Georgia, briefing members of Congress, and presenting to the UN Commission on Narcotic Drugs. According to ProPublica, he did not disclose a series of benefits from the American Kratom Association, the industry's principal lobbying group, including reimbursed travel to Arkansas, Washington, Rhode Island, Vienna and Indonesia — among them an $8,700 first-class ticket — while the University of Florida's conflict-of-interest policy requires disclosure when annual travel exceeds $5,000. ProPublica reports he listed no travel, and the university said it found no indication of non-compliance. McCurdy told ProPublica his positions rest on more than two decades of research, are not dictated by the association, and are unaffected by reimbursed expenses. Whether or not that is right in his case, it is exactly why disclosure rules exist: a legislator cannot audit the pharmacology, so the only available check is knowing who paid for the expert to be in the room and weighing the testimony accordingly.

related.title: Interest Groups & Lobbying
related.hook: Between elections, organized groups press their case to government every day. Lobbying is how that pressure is applied — and it's both a feature and a worry of democracy.

related.title: Gifts, Regulators, and the Companies They Regulate
related.hook: Two FCC officials took pricey gala tickets from Paramount while the company had billions of dollars in mergers awaiting the agency's approval. Ethics rules exist for exactly this.

related.title: Regulatory Capture
related.hook: Who protects a city's drinking water when the industry that put it at risk is also the one the regulator was built to serve? That's the problem political scientists call regulatory capture.

related.title: How Official Statistics Earn Trust
related.hook: A government statistic carries weight only because of the process behind it. When a report skips the usual methodology and review, the number stops being evidence and becomes an argument.

flashcards.prompt: Why do disclosure rules matter more than bans when experts advise legislatures?
flashcards.back_html: Legislators cannot independently verify technical claims. Disclosure lets them weight the advice, which is the only realistic check when the expertise itself is the reason the expert was invited.

flashcards.prompt: What gave one scientist policy leverage in the kratom debate, per ProPublica?

choices.text: State legislatures, Congress and a UN commission relied on him for technical expertise they lacked
He held a formal seat on the DEA's governing board
He personally wrote the state statutes at issue

flashcards.explanation_html: Influence here came from being the credible technical voice in rooms that had no other one — not from any official position.

flashcards.prompt: What did ProPublica report was left off the scientist's required disclosures?

choices.text: Industry-paid travel, including an $8,700 first-class ticket, above his university's $5,000 threshold
His academic publications on kratom pharmacology
His salary from the University of Florida

flashcards.explanation_html: The university policy requires disclosing annual travel over $5,000; ProPublica reports he listed none, while the university said it found no indication of non-compliance.
